findings.text: Solve pulls want tokens from a solver that the caller chooses
Solve pays users with a want token that has no code

The validity check accepts an order that pays zero: Code smells: `isAtomicRequestValid` checks only `atomicPrice != 0`, not that `_calculateAssetAmount` is more than zero, and `viewSolveMetaData` has no zero-price flag. — The helpers tell a solver that an order is valid when it pays zero want tokens. We found a loss of under one unit of `want` only.

One failed user transfer reverts the whole batch: Code smells: one failed `safeTransferFrom` reverts `solve`, and the function has no per-user skip. — A blacklisted user or a user who lowers the allowance makes the batch fail for the other users. The solver can remove that user and try again.

Solve does not measure what a fee-on-transfer token delivers: Code smells: `want.safeTransferFrom` and `offer.safeTransferFrom` count the amount sent, not the amount received, and `assetsToOffer` reports the full `offerAmount` to the solver. — A token that takes a fee on transfer gives the user less than the order price. We did not find a supported token that

Solve has no maximum price for the solver: Code smells: `solve` reads `atomicPrice` from storage when it runs and has no expected-price parameter. — A user can send `updateAtomicRequest` with a higher price before a pending `solve`, so a solver that does not check `assetsForWant` pays too much. We did not confirm such a solver.

A caller can close an order by naming the user as solver: Code smells: `solve` accepts `solver == users[i]`, so both transfers go from the user to the user and `offerAmount` becomes 0. — An attacker can delete the order of a smart-wallet user and move no value. This works only for a wallet with a no-op fallback and a want-token allowance.

Old orders stay fillable until the deadline: Code smells: an order stays live after the user's balance or allowance changes, and any caller can fill it. — An attacker can fill a forgotten order at its old price when the user gets offer tokens and allowance again. This needs the user to leave the order open.

Solve fills orders that pay zero want tokens: Code smells: `solve` does not check `atomicPrice == 0`, and it does not check that `assetsToUser` is more than zero after `mulDivDown` rounds down. — Any caller can take the offer tokens of an order with a zero price or a very small payout. We found only orders that the user sets, and the NatSpec do

The order struct limits the offer amount to uint96: Code smells: `offerAmount` is `uint96` and `atomicPrice` is `uint88`. — The struct limits an order to about 7.9e10 tokens with 18 decimals. We found no token where this limit causes a loss, only a failed order.

The function stores an order with a zero price: Code smells: `updateAtomicRequest` accepts `atomicPrice == 0`, but `isAtomicRequestValid` rejects the same order. — Any caller can fill the order and pay zero want tokens. Only the user can create the order, and the NatSpec documents it.
